The contextual data that gets fused with radiation measurements in SDF can be derived from a variety of sensors or sources but foremost is a description of the physical surroundings of the radiation detector(s) during measurements, the detectors’ stance within those surroundings, and when and whether there is material between the radiation detectors and potential radioactive material. This contextual data can be provided by algorithms running on camera feeds, light detection and ranging (lidar) systems, global positioning system (GPS) and/or inertial measurement units (IMUs), or the sensor system’s orientation and positioningcanbeascertainedwithinapriormap. SimultaneousLocalizationandMapping(SLAM) algorithms operating on data produced by contextual sensors are typically used to produce higher- level data products consisting of a 3D map and an instantaneous estimate of the detector system’s stance within that map [4]. Image recognition software such as semantic segmentation [5], instance segmentation [6], and object tracking [7], and the equivalent algorithms operating on lidar or camera-lidar fused data can provide additional information for SDF algorithms. SDFdiffersfrommorecommonradiationdetectiontechnologiesofradiationimagingorradiation mapping in that the latter technologies typically constrain their solutions to 2-dimensional (2D) spaces. In the case of imaging, a stationary radiation detector with imaging capabilities (typically due to Compton or coded aperture modalities) is able to achieve angular resolution in the 2D angular space surrounding the detector. Typically, this space is parameterized in the azimuth (θ) and polar (ϕ) dimensions. Examples of commercially-available imaging detectors include the H3D M400 [9] and the PhDs GeGI [10]. An example of a H3D detector system conducting data fusion with a camera is shown in Fig. 2.
